state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only

turn_history.text: Let's revisit the concept of changing values by the same proportion and how it affects the range. Think about how each plant's height would change if they were cut in half or grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each. How would these changes impact the range of the plant heights?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so if I think about it, if we cut all the plants in half, the heights would be \( 12 \mathrm{~cm}, 8.5 \mathrm{~cm}, 21 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm}, 6.5 \mathrm{~cm} \). The range would still be the same, right? But if we add \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) to each, it changes the heights to \( 27 \mathrm{~cm}, 20 \mathrm{~cm}, 45 \mathrm{~cm}, 29 \mathrm{~cm}, 16 \mathrm{~cm} \), and I think the range would change too. turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's focus on why the range changes when you add but not when you cut in half. Think about how the changes in height affect the spread of the data points. Can you see how increasing all the heights by the same amount might spread the data out more than cutting them in half?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get it a bit better now! When we cut the heights in half, the smallest and largest plants are still the same proportion apart, so the range stays the same. Is it because everything gets smaller but stays in the same order?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher fails to correct critical mathematical errors (the student incorrectly believes cutting in half keeps range constant and adding changes it, when the opposite is true), and the student ends the dialogue more confused than at the start, having reinforced the original misconception.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher asks broad, open-ended questions without breaking the problem into manageable steps or providing scaffolding adjusted to the student's specific misconception about how multiplicative versus additive transformations affect range.
